# Tulip mania (Dutch Republic, 1634–1637) — research notes
- Contract prices for rare tulip bulbs rose sharply from 1634 and collapsed in February 1637 [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulip_mania]
- 1593: Carolus Clusius planted his tulip collection in the new Hortus Botanicus of Leiden [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulip_mania]
- By 1634 speculators entered the market; by November 1636 even common bulbs rose [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulip_mania]
- Traders met in 'colleges' in taverns; some contracts changed hands five times; no bulbs were delivered [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulip_mania]
- At its height a Semper Augustus bulb sold for 10,000 guilders; a skilled artisan earned about 300 guilders a year [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulip_mania]
- 3 February 1637, Haarlem: according to a contemporary satire, an auctioneer found no buyers despite lowering the price several times; the actual circumstances are unknown [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulip_mania]
- 5 February 1637: last date of the bubble, 98 sales recorded [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulip_mania]
- 24 February 1637: the florists' guild turned contracts written after 30 November 1636 into option contracts [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulip_mania]
- The satire 'Dialogues between Waermondt and Gaergoedt' is the main source of price data [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulip_mania]
- 1841: Charles Mackay popularised the story (investors ruined, sailor who ate a bulb) [https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/24518]
- 2007: Anne Goldgar's archival study: traders were mostly wealthy merchants and craftsmen; Mackay's account is contested [https://books.google.com/books?id=gViwLbCJ7X0C] [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulip_mania]

registry.title: Tulip mania
snippets: A contemporary satire suggests that the crisis started to unravel at February 3 in Haarlem, where an auctioneer failed to find willing buyers, despite lowering the asking price several times.
The Semper Augustus was the most expensive tulip during the mania, at its height this tulip was even sold for ƒ10,000

snippets: Nobles, citizens, farmers, mechanics, sea-men, footmen, maid-servants, even chimney-sweeps and old clothes-women, dabbled in tulips.
